Imagine you slaughter a cow. It has a thick skin covering its body — that skin is called a hide. Now, what if you removed that skin, scraped off all the hair and fat from it, and then simply dried it in the sun without doing anything else to it? What you'd end up with is rawhide.

So, rawhide is the untreated, dried skin of an animal — most commonly cattle — that has been cleaned but has not gone through any chemical process to soften or preserve it further.

The word itself is straightforward once you break it apart: raw means untreated or unprocessed, and hide means the skin of an animal. Put them together: untreated animal skin.
Rawhide vs. Leather — The Most Important Distinction

To truly understand rawhide, you must compare it to leather, because people often confuse the two.

Leather is animal hide that has been put through a process called tanning — a chemical treatment (using substances like tannin from tree bark, or modern industrial chemicals) that transforms the raw skin into something soft, smooth, flexible, and resistant to water and decay. Leather is what your belt, your shoes, your wallet, and your jacket are made of. It stays soft and flexible even after it dries.

Rawhide, on the other hand, has never been tanned. It skips that entire process. It is simply cleaned and dried — nothing more.

This is why rawhide and leather have completely different properties.

Rawhide behaves in a way that is quite remarkable, and understanding this behavior is the key to understanding why people use it.

When rawhide is wet or damp:
It is soft, pliable, and almost clay-like. You can bend it, shape it, mold it, wrap it around things, and stretch it. It is very workable in this state.

When rawhide dries completely:
It becomes extremely hard and rigid — almost like a piece of stiff plastic or a wooden board. It shrinks slightly as it dries. And this hardened form is incredibly tough and strong — difficult to cut or break.

The critical behavior: This cycle can be reversed. If you soak dry rawhide in water, it becomes soft and pliable again. Dry it out, and it hardens again. This wet-soft / dry-hard behavior is the defining feature of rawhide, and it is the reason humans have found it so extraordinarily useful throughout history.

Rawhide is typically off-white, cream, or pale yellowish in color — almost translucent when you hold it up to the light. It does not have the rich smell of leather. When very dry, it can be odorless or have a faint animal smell.

Because of its unique properties, rawhide has been used by humans all over the world for thousands of years. Here are its main uses:

1. As a binding material
This is perhaps the oldest and most clever use of rawhide. When you wrap wet rawhide tightly around two pieces of wood or bone — say, a stone axe head onto a wooden handle — and then let it dry, it contracts and hardens into an incredibly tight, rigid grip. It becomes better than a clamp, better than a knot. Ancient peoples used this technique to make tools, weapons, and structures. The drying process does the "tightening" for you automatically.

2. For making whips
Long strips of rawhide can be braided and formed into whips. Because rawhide is so tough, it makes an effective and durable whip. The classic long cattle whip that you picture cowboys and ranchers using is traditionally made from rawhide.

3. Drumheads
Traditional drums from many cultures — Native American drums, African drums, and others — use rawhide stretched across a wooden frame. When the hide dries and tightens, it creates a taut surface that produces a resonant sound when struck. The tightness of the stretched rawhide determines the pitch and tone of the drum.

4. Dog chews
This is the most common use of rawhide in modern everyday life. Pet stores sell rawhide chews — sticks, rolls, twisted pieces, and shaped treats — made from the inner layer of cattle hide, sometimes pressed and flavored. Dogs love to chew on them. They start firm but soften with the dog's saliva, making them safe to gnaw on for extended periods. If you've ever bought a chew treat for a dog, there is a very good chance it was rawhide.

5. Footwear
Native American peoples historically made the soles of their moccasins from rawhide because it is so tough and hard-wearing. The hardness of dried rawhide made it excellent as a protective sole for the foot.

6. Shields and armor
Warriors in many ancient cultures used hardened rawhide to make shields. Layers of rawhide were shaped while wet and allowed to dry into rigid, hard pieces. Hardened rawhide can deflect blows and was a practical alternative to metal armor, which was expensive and heavy.

7. Containers and boxes
Native American peoples (especially of the Great Plains) made containers called parfleches from folded rawhide. These were like envelopes or boxes made by folding flat sheets of rawhide while it was wet and letting it dry into a rigid container. They were used to store and transport food, clothing, and other belongings. Because rawhide is so tough, these containers were durable and practical.

8. Snowshoe frames and lacing
Traditional snowshoes were made with a wooden or bone frame, laced with strips of rawhide. The webbing of the snowshoe that distributes your weight across the snow was woven from rawhide strips.

9. Hide glue
Rawhide can be boiled in water for a long time until it dissolves and produces a thick, sticky liquid. When this liquid cools, it sets into a very strong glue — called hide glue. This glue has been used for centuries in woodworking, furniture-making, and musical instrument construction (like violins and guitars). Some craftspeople still use it today because it has properties that modern glues do not replicate exactly.

10. Saddles and horse tack
In traditional Western saddle-making (the kind used by cowboys and ranchers), rawhide is used in specific parts of the saddle — particularly as a covering for the saddle tree (the inner frame of the saddle) and for certain bindings. It is prized because when it dries on the frame, it becomes hard and creates a tough, reinforced structure.

Rawhide's greatest weakness is also tied to its defining property: it is not waterproof.

Because rawhide was never tanned, it has not been made resistant to water. When it gets wet, it softens — which is sometimes desirable (for reshaping it) but often a problem. Rawhide used outdoors over time will weaken, soften, and eventually begin to rot if it stays wet. Leather, by contrast, is much more resistant to water and decay because tanning changes the structure of the hide at a chemical level.

This is why, in applications where lasting exposure to moisture is expected, people prefer leather over rawhide.

Think of it this way: the hide of a cow can take several paths after the animal is slaughtered.

  • If you tan it → you get leather (soft, flexible, durable, water-resistant).
  • If you simply clean it and dry it without tanning → you get rawhide (stiff, hard when dry, soft when wet, not water-resistant).
  • If you boil rawhide in water for long enough → you get hide glue.

Rawhide sits at the simplest, most natural stage of processing animal hide. It is the unsophisticated, unchemically-altered form of the skin — which, paradoxically, makes it incredibly useful precisely because of its simple, dramatic wet-soft / dry-hard behavior.

Rawhide is the untanned, dried skin of an animal (usually cattle) that has been cleaned and preserved through drying alone, without any chemical treatment. When wet, it is soft and moldable; when dry, it becomes rock-hard and extremely tough. This unique property has made it one of the most practical materials in human history, used for binding tools, making drums, crafting whips and shields, forming containers, producing glue, and — most famously in the modern world — as chew treats for dogs.
